title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 220: The Demise of the Mental Map
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 220 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Demise of the Mental Map: Spatial Cognition in the Digital Age

Paragraph 1. For tens of thousands of years, navigating the physical world was an essential survival skill for humans. Whether crossing open plains or sailing across oceans using the stars, our ancestors depended on internal mental maps created inside the brain. Over the past twenty years, however, widespread smartphone GPS apps have changed this ancient habit. Instead of studying nearby hills, rivers, and buildings, modern travellers simply obey voice directions without thinking actively about space.

Paragraph 2. The brain's navigation control centre is the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped organ deep inside the brain. In the early 2000s, British neuroscientist Dr. Eleanor Maguire studied the brains of licensed London taxi drivers. To earn a license, drivers must spend three to four years memorizing twenty-five thousand streets and thousands of buildings around central London. Maguire discovered that qualified taxi drivers had a noticeably larger back hippocampus than ordinary adults, and its size grew with their years of driving.

Paragraph 3. Under turn-by-turn GPS guidance, however, brain scans reveal that activity inside the hippocampus and decision-making areas drops sharply. Unlike real navigation, which requires comparing landmarks and predicting turns, following digital arrows needs only quick automatic reactions. As a result, users develop 'tunnel vision' and ignore side streets, often becoming completely confused in familiar neighbourhoods if their battery dies.

Paragraph 4. Geriatric doctors warn that losing active spatial skills may bring long-term health risks. Medical studies confirm that the hippocampus is among the first brain parts damaged by Alzheimer's disease, with spatial confusion often appearing as the earliest warning sign. Because lifelong mental exercise builds brain resilience, relying heavily on GPS could leave ageing brains less protected against memory loss.

Paragraph 5. To protect spatial health, psychologists suggest turning off GPS on familiar local roads so the brain must notice landmarks and estimate distances independently. Meanwhile, software engineers are designing improved navigation apps that give helpful landmark clues—such as 'turn right after the stone cathedral'—or wider overview maps instead of blind turn-by-turn commands.
